title: Design In-Memory File System
description:
Design a data structure that simulates an in-memory file system.

Implement the `FileSystem` class:
- `FileSystem()` initializes the object of the system with an empty root directory `"/"`.
- `List<String> ls(String path)`:
  - If `path` is a file path, returns a list containing only this file's name.
  - If `path` is a directory path, returns the list of file and directory names directly inside this directory, sorted in **lexicographical order**.
- `void mkdir(String path)` creates a new directory at the given `path`. If middle directories in the path do not exist, create them as well.
- `void addContentToFile(String filePath, String content)`:
  - If `filePath` does not exist, creates that file containing `content`.
  - If `filePath` already exists, appends `content` to its existing content.
- `String readContentFromFile(String filePath)` returns the content of the file at `filePath`.
constraints: path and filePath are absolute paths starting with '/' and do not end with '/' except when the path is '/' itself.
All directory and file names consist only of lowercase English letters, and no two entries in the same directory share the same name.
All operations are valid: ls is only called on existing paths, readContentFromFile is only called on existing files, and mkdir is never called on an existing file path.
At most 300 calls in total will be made to ls, mkdir, addContentToFile, and readContentFromFile.
hints: Model the directory hierarchy as a trie where each edge is a path segment (directory or file name) rather than a single character.
Each trie node stores a map from child name to child node, a boolean flag marking whether it is a file, and a string buffer holding its content if it is a file.
Using a sorted map (such as TreeMap in Java) or sorting child keys on ls ensures directory listings are always returned in lexicographical order.

examples.explanation: Initially "/" is empty. After mkdir("/a/b/c") and adding "hello" to "/a/b/c/d", ls("/") returns ["a"] and reading "/a/b/c/d" returns "hello".
ls("/") returns files and directories sorted lexicographically as ["a","m","z"]. Appending to "/m" concatenates the content, and ls("/m") returns only the file name ["m"].

timeComplexity: O(P + K log K) for ls, O(P + C) for file ops
